name: Strum
tagline: A guitar learning app that walks you through chords, strumming patterns and songs, and listens to you play.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The mechanical parts of a guitar trainer are surprisingly tractable: chord diagrams are data, a metronome is a timer, and a scrolling chord chart is a div that moves. Even rough mic listening works, a chromagram plus template matching will tell you whether you just played G or Em with decent accuracy in a quiet room. What an agent cannot produce in one session is the songbook: licensed song arrangements, correct chord-over-lyric timing, and a lesson path that ramps difficulty in an order that does not make a beginner quit. So you get a real practice tool for songs you already have charts for, and nothing that teaches you what to learn next. That gap is the product.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app that shows chord diagrams and a scrolling chord chart over a metronome click, then uses the mic to check whether the chord you played matches the one on screen.
requirements: A laptop with a working microphone, and a browser that grants mic access over localhost
Your own chord charts, entered as JSON or plain text
A quiet room, mic chord detection falls apart with background noise
Optional: a USB audio interface if you want to plug the guitar in directly
whatYouLose: The song catalog, and the licensing that lets it exist legally
A curated beginner-to-intermediate lesson path, which is most of what you are actually paying for
A native mobile app that runs on the phone propped against your guitar case
Robust pitch and chord detection tuned across cheap phone mics, room noise and bad tuning
Streaks, progress tracking and the mild guilt that makes people practice at all
moatNotes: Song arrangements are licensed, and the lesson ordering is accumulated teaching judgment, not a feature list.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the hard part of learning guitar is not having a chord chart, it is knowing which twelve songs to play in which order so that your hands stop hurting before you stop caring. A paid app sells sequencing, licensed arrangements you can actually play along to, and a phone app that works while you are sitting on the edge of the bed. A self-built trainer gives you the drill loop but leaves you as your own curriculum designer, which is exactly the job a beginner is worst at.
notes: Great weekend build if you already know what you want to practice, useless if you do not.
prompt:
Build a local-only guitar practice web app. No accounts, no backend, no telemetry.

Stack: Vite + TypeScript + vanilla DOM, Web Audio API, Tailwind for styling. No React, no server. Everything runs from `npm run dev` in the browser. State persists to localStorage only.

Features, in scope:
1. A chord library as a typed data file: at least 24 open chords (major, minor, 7th) with fret/finger positions. Render each as an SVG chord diagram (6 strings, 5 frets, dots, muted strings, finger numbers).
2. A song format: plain text files in `/songs` where lines alternate chord lines and lyric lines, plus a header with title, BPM and time signature. Parse them at load. Ship three public-domain examples I can copy.
3. Song player: a scrolling chord chart that highlights the current bar in time with a Web Audio metronome (accurate scheduling via AudioContext.currentTime, not setInterval drift). Controls: play/pause, BPM slider, count-in, loop a selected section.
4. Practice mode: show one chord diagram at a time, click on the beat, and ask the user to switch chords on the change. Configurable chord set and switch interval.
5. Mic listener: getUserMedia, AnalyserNode, compute a 12-bin chromagram from the FFT, match it against precomputed chord templates by cosine similarity, and show the best guess plus a confidence bar. Mark the on-screen target chord green when it matches for 3 consecutive frames. Be honest in the UI that this is approximate.
6. A chromatic tuner: autocorrelation pitch detection, nearest note name, cents off, needle display.
7. A practice log: minutes practiced per day from actual play time, stored in localStorage, shown as a simple 12-week grid.

Out of scope: any song content I do not supply myself, user accounts, cloud sync, audio recording or upload, mobile app packaging, tab rendering, backing tracks.

Quality bar: mic access requested only when the listener or tuner is opened, clear permission-denied fallback, keyboard shortcuts for play/pause and BPM, works offline after first load. Put nothing in .env because there are no secrets. Write a README that explains the song file format in ten lines or fewer.
